newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada forestry firms table new framework in talks.
newsitem.headline: Canada forestry firms table new framework in talks.

text.p: Canadian forestry firms tabled a new set of proposals to continue talks with the union representing lumber workers in British Columbia on Tuesday, forestalling the chance of a strike vote, the union said.

The bargaining agent for 65 coastal forestry companies, called Forest Industrial Relations, amended its June 23 framework which suggested a five-year collective agreement with no pay hikes or cuts to members of the IWA-Canada union.

Instead, on Tuesday the bargaining agent proposed a three- year deal with the possibility of wage raises in the second and third terms, depending on the companies' ability to pay, union president David Haggard told Reuters.
The two sides have been in talks since early May but discussions intensified since a collective agreement expired on June 14.
Haggard said that "I'm cautiously optimistic that with those types of moves, we can get a collective agreement."
He added the new framework pushed back a possible strike vote "for this week."
"We're hoping to get back with them sometime tomorrow with a counterproposal," Haggard said.

Forest Industrial Relations officials were not available to comment. But the forestry companies have said they cannot bear significant cost increases given recent losses due to weak commodity prices and high operating costs.
British Columbia's publicly held lumber firms are major exporters to the United States and Japan. The west coast Canadian province fills about 20 percent of the U.S. lumber market's needs each year.
IWA-Canada represents about 29,000 unionized workers in British Columbia, a region which has traditionally relied on the forestry and paper products sector for much of its economic growth.

One bone of contention is pension fund contributions -- both sides are debating the companies' desire for some relief from contributions, Haggard said. Currently the pension fund is worth about C$1.4 billion ($1.01 billion.)
Haggard added that the union was planning to speed through talks instead of dragging them out until September or later in the fall as usual.
"It's our intention to hopefully have a collective agreement by the end of July," Haggard said.
